newsitem.title: USA: Fall harvest glut pulls down U.S. farm price index.
newsitem.headline: Fall harvest glut pulls down U.S. farm price index.

text.p: Lower prices for broilers, wheat, cotton and hogs helped depress a government index of farm prices by 2.8 percent for February, the U.S. Agriculture Department said Friday.
The index, a gauge of prices paid to farmers for their crops and livestock, had a February reading of 105, down 2.8 percent from January and 0.9 percent from a year earlier.
Soybeans, tobacco, hay and tomato prices rose during February. Soybeans averaged $7.37 a bushel, up 24 cents.
"Expected tighter supplies at the end of the marketing year has been the major factor in the price increase," USDA said.
Wheat prices fell 12 cents from January to average $3.91 a bushel. Increased competition for export sales weighed on U.S. prices.
Cotton sold for an average 66.7 cents a lb in February, down 1.1 cent from January. At 39.1 cents a lb, broiler prices were down 1.3 cents.
With hog slaughter running five percent above year-ago levels, prices dipped by $1.20 per 100 lbs to average $52.60. Nonetheless, hog prices were far above the $46.50 average of February 1996.
Cattle prices also fell in February to average $61.20, a 20-cent drop from January but $3.30 higher than a year ago. Large cattle supplies dampened prices.
The all-milk price fell 10 cents during February to average $13.30 per 100 lbs. Milk output was below the year-earlier level but demand also declined.
Hay rose to $105 a short ton in February, compared to January's average of $99.70 a ton. Tomatos reached an average $45.10 per 100 lbs, up $13.70.
Tobacco prices averaged $2.07 a lb, compared to $2.10 in January.
